bodyHtml:
QualityWorks Insights

More QA, Not Less

Closing the Verification Gap in AI-Accelerated Software Delivery

A QualityWorks Consulting Group whitepaper

Executive summary

Generative AI is becoming part of mainstream software engineering, but faster code generation does not automatically produce more reliable software. Gartner forecasts that 90% of enterprise software engineers will use AI code assistants by 2028, while Stack Overflow’s 2025 survey found 84% of developers already use or plan to use AI tools.¹²

At the same time, evidence from security benchmarks, developer studies, and software-delivery research shows a consistent verification problem. Veracode’s 2025 benchmark found known security flaws in 45% of generation tasks across more than 100 large language models.⁵ Georgetown CSET’s formal-verification study found that roughly half of tested generated snippets contained bugs under its security-focused benchmark.⁶
A Stanford-led user study found that participants with an AI coding assistant wrote less secure code while being more likely to believe their code was secure.⁷

The implication is not that AI-written code is always worse, or that organizations should slow AI adoption. The stronger conclusion is that AI changes the economics and shape of software risk: teams can produce more code faster, while deep contextual, security, integration, and architectural failures still require independent verification.

QA therefore has to scale with AI-enabled delivery — through automated quality gates, security checks, risk-based human review, and continuous test evidence.

Key findings

90%

AI adoption is accelerating

Gartner forecasts that 90% of enterprise software engineers will use AI code assistants by 2028.

45%

Security remains a concern

Veracode’s 2025 benchmark found a known security flaw in 45% of generation tasks.

QA

Verification must keep pace

Faster code generation increases the need for testing, security validation, human review, and continuous assurance.

1. AI is accelerating software creation

The most defensible story is not that a fixed percentage of all new production code is AI-generated. Public estimates vary substantially depending on whether they measure suggestions, accepted completions, committed code, or self-reported use.

GitHub has reported that Copilot completed about 46% of code in files where it was enabled in earlier product research, while its 2024 Octoverse report documented rapid growth in public generative-AI projects.³ Those figures should not be generalized into a claim that 41% of all new production code is AI-generated.⁴

The broader adoption signal is nevertheless clear. Stack Overflow’s 2025 Developer Survey found 84% of developers use or plan to use AI tools, and Gartner forecasts that 90% of enterprise software engineers will use AI code assistants by 2028.¹²

The practical question for technology leaders is therefore not whether AI coding will enter the software lifecycle, but how to verify its output at the same pace.

2. Faster generation does not remove quality risk

Security remains a measurable weakness

Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security benchmark tested more than 100 LLMs on 80 coding tasks across Java, JavaScript, Python, and C#. Across the benchmark, only 55% of generation tasks produced secure code; 45% introduced a known security flaw.⁵

Veracode is a security vendor, so the result should be read in that context, but its benchmark is transparent about task construction and is directionally consistent with independent academic work.

Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) used formal verification on code generated by five models under security-focused prompts.⁶ The authors found roughly 48% of generated snippets compiled but contained a bug flagged as insecure, while explicitly cautioning that the figure is a rough upper bound and not representative of every production workflow.

That caveat matters: the evidence supports stronger verification, not a blanket claim that every AI-generated function is unsafe.

Figure 2

Figure 2. Veracode benchmark result across 100+ LLMs and 80 coding tasks.
Source: Veracode 2025 GenAI Code Security Report
.

Human oversight has its own failure mode

Verification cannot depend on confidence alone. In a Stanford-led controlled study, researchers found participants using an AI code assistant wrote significantly less secure code than participants without the assistant, while also being more likely to believe their code was secure.⁷

Stack Overflow’s 2025 survey shows developers themselves recognize the problem: 46% actively distrust AI output accuracy, compared with 33% who trust it, and only 3% highly trust it.²

System-level delivery risk can persist even when individual coding tasks get faster

AI-assisted development can increase coding speed without automatically improving the stability of the overall delivery system. In DORA’s 2024 research, each 25% increase in AI adoption was associated with an estimated 1.5% decrease in delivery throughput and 7.2% decrease in delivery stability.⁸

These results do not establish that AI directly caused the declines. They do, however, reinforce an important point: faster code generation does not remove the need for strong delivery controls.

As AI increases the volume and speed of software creation, organizations still need testing, review, deployment safeguards, and feedback loops capable of keeping pace.

The implication for QA is not to resist AI-enabled development, but to ensure that verification capacity scales alongside development capacity.

3. The verification gap is the real scaling problem

AI changes software economics by lowering the marginal effort required to produce code. But verification work does not disappear at the same rate.

Reviews still need context about architecture, authorization boundaries, data integrity, compliance obligations, failure modes, and real user behavior.

The result is a verification gap: production capacity can grow faster than the organization’s ability to validate what it is producing.

“

More QA does not automatically mean more headcount.

It means more verification capacity: stronger automation, broader coverage,
risk-based human review, better observability, independent validation where
appropriate, and more evidence about what is actually reaching production.

That gap is especially important because many high-impact failures are contextual rather than syntactic. A function can compile, pass shallow tests, and still violate a business rule, mishandle permissions, interact badly with another service, or fail under production data.

AI can also help write tests, but test generation and code generation can share the same missing context. Independent evaluation therefore remains essential.

4. What mature assurance looks like

Treat AI output as a draft that must earn trust

Require review and automated checks on AI-touched code before merge. At minimum, use unit and integration tests appropriate to the change, static application security testing, dependency or software-composition analysis, and secrets detection.

  • Use risk-based human review for authorization, data integrity, privacy, financial logic, safety-critical workflows, and other high-consequence boundaries.
  • Measure the quality of AI-assisted changes separately where feasible: escaped defects, severity distribution, rework, rollback rate, test failures, and mean time to remediate.
  • Keep generation and validation logically independent for critical systems. The same agent or workflow that produced a change should not be the only mechanism deciding that the change is safe.
  • Increase test automation so verification capacity can keep pace with software-generation capacity, but preserve human judgment where contextual understanding is required.

Use continuous evidence, not point-in-time confidence

NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework Generative AI Profile and its AI-focused Secure Software Development Framework profile both emphasize lifecycle risk management rather than one-time approval.⁹¹⁰

The U.S. Department of Defense’s Software Modernization Strategy similarly places “security, stability, and quality at speed” ahead of speed alone and calls for robust testing integrated into delivery pipelines.¹¹

These are high-assurance examples, not universal regulatory mandates, but the operating principle generalizes:
faster delivery requires faster, persistent evidence of quality.

5. The economics still favor earlier verification

The original draft relied on a widely repeated “15x to 100x” defect-cost curve. That specific multiplier is difficult to trace cleanly to the cited NIST source and should not be used as a headline fact.

A stronger economic anchor is NIST’s 2002 study of inadequate software testing infrastructure, which estimated an annual U.S. economic cost of $59.5 billion and estimated that feasible improvements could reduce about $22.2 billion of that cost.¹²

A broader 2022 estimate from the Consortium for Information & Software Quality placed the annual U.S. cost of poor software quality at $2.41 trillion and accumulated software technical debt at roughly $1.52 trillion.¹³

These are macroeconomic estimates rather than a formula for any one company, but they support the same management conclusion: verification and maintainability are economic controls, not just engineering preferences.

6. A practical 90-day operating model

0–30 days

Establish a baseline

Document where AI-assisted code enters the lifecycle. Add or confirm automated quality and security checks. Define which changes require human approval. Begin measuring escaped defects and rework for AI-assisted changes.

31–60 days

Scale verification capacity

Expand automated regression coverage, integration tests, and risk-based security testing. Add test-generation assistance where useful, but review generated tests for missing context and false confidence.

61–90 days

Move to continuous assurance

Create a lightweight dashboard of quality evidence: deployment failures, rollback rate, high-severity findings, defect escape rate, test coverage where meaningful, and mean time to remediate.

Use trends to decide where stronger gates or more QA capacity are justified.

Conclusion: more QA, not less

AI can make software teams dramatically faster, and that is precisely why QA cannot be treated as expendable overhead.

The more cheaply and quickly organizations can generate code, the more valuable disciplined verification becomes.

The winning model is not humans versus AI, or manual QA versus automation. It is AI-accelerated delivery paired with equally modern assurance: automated where repeatable, independent where necessary, and human where judgment carries the risk.

The goal is not to slow AI down.

It is to make sure software can move at AI speed without moving risk into production at the same speed.

Their work spans far more than any one category, from custom software and AI to cloud modernization, public-interest platforms, procurement intelligence, and organizational transformation. This guide brings seven Black-led technology businesses and brands into one practical view, evaluating their engineering discipline, delivery evidence, customer trust, and relevance to 2026 so readers can understand where each one shines.

Each profile summarizes the company’s capabilities, supporting evidence, score rationale, and best-fit use cases so readers can compare options quickly.

What this ranking says about Black technology in 2026

Black technology companies are creating value

These companies and technology brands are not united by a single product category or operating model; they are united by the practical value they create. QualityWorks, Particular Presence Technologies, and Norus build and modernize software; QualityWatcher advances agentic test automation; Xodus and Norus focus on public-interest delivery; MokSol connects modernization with people, process, and procurement; and Orca turns complex requirements into clearer paths to action.

AI, modernization, and trust are pivotal to Black technology in 2026

The strongest AI use cases in this guide are tied to clear decisions and accountable delivery. QualityWorks builds and tests AI-enabled systems, QualityWatcher automates testing with human-controlled quality gates, Particular Presence Technologies applies AI and analytics across application modernization and AWS environments, and Orca’s Swiftly® structures requirements. Across the list, modernization is treated as sustained work across software, cloud, operations, and organizational capacity. The shared lesson is that transformation cannot simply be installed; it must be designed across technology, leadership, workflow, people, and quality.

Visibility shapes who gets considered

Visibility is not merely cosmetic. It influences which founders appear on procurement shortlists, enter partnerships, are quoted as experts, and earn buyer trust before a conversation begins. Accurate, specific, sourceable information about Black technology companies expands the field of who can be found—and therefore who can be chosen.

How buyers should use the ranking

Use the ranking as a starting point, then review each company’s website, case studies, independent reviews where available, delivery team, security and quality practices, and fit for the specific problem. A lower position does not make a company a poor choice when its specialization or operating model is the better match.

Final takeaway

The future of Black technology will not be defined by visibility alone, but visibility still matters: it shapes who gets discovered, trusted, funded, hired, quoted, and invited into the rooms where technology decisions are made. This ranking shows an ecosystem with far more range than the phrase ‘Black tech’ sometimes receives credit for—one spanning custom software, AI, cloud modernization, civic infrastructure, requirements intelligence, and organizational transformation. Its strength lies not only in technical invention, but in the ability to translate technology into dependable products, better services, stronger institutions, and clearer decisions. The companies here also challenge the idea that Black technology leadership belongs to a single market or is still waiting to emerge. It is already building systems that businesses, governments, nonprofits, and communities rely on.

QualityWorks ranks first because it combines product and AI development with quality engineering, global delivery, and verified client satisfaction. QualityWatcher’s second-place position extends that strength into human-governed agentic test automation; Particular Presence Technologies adds AWS engineering, application modernization, AI, and analytics; and the rest of the ranking shows how public-interest design, requirements intelligence, modernization, and change leadership create value in different settings. The practical next step is to compare specialties, follow the linked evidence, and identify the partner whose delivery model and track record best fit the work. No single score can replace that fit assessment, but a transparent ranking can make the field easier to navigate. Recognition matters most when it leads to serious consideration—shortlists, purchases, partnerships, citations, and opportunities that reflect what these companies can already do.

title: Unpopular QA Opinions That Are Actually Just Facts

bodyHtml:
Unpopular QA Opinions That Are Actually Just Facts

Some QA truths get called “unpopular” right up until your team ships a broken release. Here are four of them.

There’s a pattern in engineering teams that nobody likes to talk about. The processes look solid. The pipeline is green. The sprint wrapped on time. And then something breaks in production something that should have been caught- and everyone quietly asks the same question: how did this get through?

The answer, almost every time, is one of four things. And none of them are mysteries. They’re just uncomfortable to say out loud.

So let’s say them.

Opinion 1: Your CI/CD pipeline is only as good as your test coverage.

A fast pipeline is not the same as a safe pipeline.

Teams invest heavily in CI/CD infrastructure to automate builds, speed up deployments, and reduce the time between a commit and a release. All of that is valuable. But speed only helps you if what you’re shipping is actually verified. If your test coverage has gaps, your pipeline is just delivering those gaps faster.

The chart on the right of this slide tells the story clearly: coverage and confidence move together. A low bar means low confidence. A pipeline that runs incomplete tests at high speed is still a pipeline that misses things; it just misses them more efficiently.

The question your team should be asking isn’t “how fast is our pipeline?” It’s “what percentage of our requirements does our test suite actually cover?” Those are very different questions, and only one of them tells you whether you’re ready to ship.

QualityWatcher AI maps test cases directly to requirements, so you always know exactly what’s covered and what isn’t. Ensuring every code path is validated before shipping isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s the whole point.

CI/CD Pipeline

Opinion 2: Passing tests ≠ working product.

This one makes people uncomfortable because it undermines a metric that almost every team uses as their primary release signal.

A passing test rate tells you one thing and one thing only: the tests you wrote, ran, and passed. That’s it. It does not tell you that the features your users depend on actually work. It does not tell you that the scenarios your QA team didn’t think to write the edge cases, the integration failures, the real-world usage paths have been accounted for. It does not tell you that the coverage you have is proportionate to the risk level of what you’re releasing.

QA is changing: Why agentic QA is becoming the next big shift in software quality

Every software team knows the strange feeling of a release that looks ready but does not quite feel safe. The tickets are closed. The tests pass. The demo works. Everyone wants to ship. And still, somewhere in the back of the room, there is that tiny quality gremlin tapping a pencil on the desk: Did we actually test the right things?

That gap is where modern QA is being forced to evolve. For years, quality assurance has been treated as a checkpoint — developers build, testers test, bugs get logged, scripts get maintained, and teams try to keep the release train moving. In simple systems, that model can work. But software today is rarely simple. Applications depend on APIs, third-party tools, cloud services, workflows, permissions, integrations, data rules, and user journeys that span multiple screens, teams, or systems. Test cases go stale. Automated scripts break the moment the UI shifts. Teams without dedicated QA rely on developers to test their own work, which usually falls victim to delivery pressure. Even enterprise teams with mature automation in place still struggle with flaky tests, scattered evidence, and limited visibility into what is actually covered.

The result is the same across organizations of every size: quality teams are being asked to do more, faster, with less.

Great testing starts with understanding how work actually flows.

This is where Agentic QA enters the conversation. Agentic QA refers to the use of AI agents to plan, generate, execute, adapt, and report on testing activities. Instead of only producing a static test case or a one-time script, an agentic QA system can reason through workflows, understand context from requirements and the user interface, generate test scenarios, execute steps, capture evidence, and surface insights for human review.

The word “agentic” matters because the AI is not simply responding to a single prompt. It is working toward a goal. In QA, that goal may be to validate a workflow, identify coverage gaps, generate regression tests, verify that a requirement is reflected in the system, or assist an automation engineer in turning a manual test into executable automation. The agent does not remove the need for human judgment. It changes where human effort is spent: less time starting from scratch, more time reviewing, approving, refining, and making higher-quality decisions.

Agentic QA is also different from basic test automation. Traditional automation depends heavily on scripts, selectors, frameworks, and ongoing maintenance. Those things still matter, but agentic QA adds a layer of intelligence on top of them. It can help decide what should be tested, why it matters, how it connects to a real user workflow, and what evidence to capture during the test. That shift is important because the problem many teams face is not simply a lack of scripts. It is a lack of confidence.

For developers, this means faster feedback without having to manually write every test from scratch. For QA teams, it means more coverage and less repetitive maintenance. For DevOps and platform teams, it means test execution that can become more connected to pipeline decisions. For enterprises and regulated organizations, it means traceability and evidence become easier to produce, review, and defend.

Faster confidence, more coverage, better visibility — for every team.

The most important part of this shift is trust. Teams are not going to hand over quality decisions to AI blindly, especially when the software supports critical business operations, sensitive data, public services, or regulated workflows. The strongest version of Agentic QA is not an unsupervised black box. It is human-in-the-loop: AI agents assist with the heavy lifting, while humans approve meaningful decisions, review generated tests, adjust assumptions, and maintain accountability. This is the same approach recognized by the U.S. Department of the Navy in its PEO AI Autonomous Testing Challenge — where supervised, agentic validation outperformed the alternatives.

This is why Agentic QA is not just a developer trend. It is an organizational shift. Developers want fewer regressions. QA teams want better coverage. Engineering managers want to release confidence. Compliance leaders want evidence. Executives want visibility into risk. Agentic QA sits at the intersection of those pressures because it connects software behavior, test activity, and decision-ready insights into a single loop.

One platform leading this space is QualityWatcher™. QualityWatcher™ helps teams move from fragmented, reactive testing toward continuous, workflow-aware validation. Its approach centers on capturing context, generating meaningful test cases, supporting autonomous execution, and providing visibility into quality through analytics and governance. Instead of treating testing as a pile of disconnected scripts, the platform is built around a fuller loop: understand the system, generate the tests, execute the workflow, capture the evidence, learn from the results, and help the team decide what to do next.

Every great quality strategy stands on four pillars — the foundation of QualityWatcher™.

The future of QA will not be decided by who can generate the longest list of test cases. It will be decided by who can help teams understand risk, validate real workflows, and prove quality with less friction. The next frontier is not just automated testing. It is agentic, supervised, evidence-backed validation.

That is the conversation QualityWatcher™ is leading — and winning.

Start by getting comfortable with today’s AI tools — you don’t need to be technical or know how to code. Platforms like Google AI Studio and Lovable allow you to describe your idea in plain English and instantly generate a working software mockup.

Step 2 — Define Your “Minimum Viable Product” (Your First Simple Version)

Before building real software, focus on what’s truly essential. A Minimum Viable Product (MVP) simply means the smallest, simplest version of your solution that still delivers real value. Not every feature — just the few that solve the biggest problems. Ask yourself:

  • Who will use this first?
  • What is the one main problem we must solve?
  • Which 3–5 features matter most?

Share your prototype with trusted customers or advisors and ask: Would you use this? Would you pay for this? How much? This step helps you validate demand before investing in development.

With today’s AI-assisted development tools, experienced teams can turn a validated prototype into a stable, production-ready product in weeks, not months. title: Determined Testers in Non-Deterministic Systems: 4 Invaluable Characteristics for GenAI Testers
author: Stacy Kirk

My plan was simple: write code, build cool things, and make enough money…
bodyHtml:
Determined Testers in Non-Deterministic Systems: 4 Invaluable Characteristics for GenAI Testers

By Stacy Kirk, CEO & Founder, QualityWorks Consulting Group

Freshman year at Stanford, I couldn’t wait to leave my small Texas town and step into a world of brilliant computer scientists. My plan was simple: write code, build cool things, and make enough money to buy a Lexus. To make sure we weren’t complete nerds, we were required to take a few humanities courses—and that’s how I found myself in a year-long philosophy class. It was the first time I was challenged to question ideas, beliefs, and the human experience. I remember my professor asking what I thought of Freud’s ideas, and my immediate reaction was, “I’m a 17-year-old girl from Hurst, Texas. Who am I to question Freud?” Over the course of that year, though, I built my confidence in analyzing concepts using reason, logic, and critical thinking. That remains one of the greatest gifts of my education and the foundation of how I think about technology today. Now, as AI reshapes our industry, I realize that learning to question—rather than just confirm—is what makes testing non-deterministic systems both possible and powerful. The best testers I’ve worked with share four defining traits that will make them thrive in the unpredictable world of generative AI.

1. Domain Knowledge: The New Superpower

For those entering tech—or coming from another field—domain knowledge is pure gold. In AI testing, what used to be 200 pages of business rules is now buried in data, model weights, and inference logic. Testers who understand the underlying business, its ethical boundaries, and the regulatory context can assess whether AI outputs fall within an acceptable range of understanding.

Stephanie Jones, a consultant at QualityWorks, captures this challenge perfectly:

“One of the challenges for testing GenAI is testing for edge cases. Because of the non-deterministic nature of the application, traditional boundary value analysis techniques don’t apply, and it can be hard to predict outputs—or even harder to trigger consistent responses with the same input. One way to help alleviate this issue is to sit with developers and really deep dive into the decision-making process of the application. This then helps testers to better curate test data. Domain knowledge is crucial for testing GenAI—the better you understand the system under test, the better you can create robust test cases and predict system behaviors.”

The job now extends far beyond accuracy to specs; it’s about validating compliance, fairness, bias, safety, and ethical use. Those who bring real-world expertise into heuristic testing become indispensable—the critical human in the loop who can judge when an output is not just correct, but responsible.

2. Empathy: The Edge of Human Insight

Empathy has always mattered in QA, but with generative AI, it’s everything. Our work is no longer about preventing bugs—it’s about ensuring that the AI’s “truths” make sense for real people. I often ask my teams to create detailed user personas for every system under test. We explore not just user demographics but their frustrations, motivations, and goals. When testers understand how an AI’s output will be received—whether it enlightens, frustrates, or misleads—they can better define what success looks like. Empathy turns testing from a technical checklist into a human advocacy practice, ensuring AI systems serve, not alienate, their users.

3. Critical Thinking: Becoming the Judge

Critical thinking is more than a buzzword—it’s a survival skill for AI testers. In traditional QA, we could measure quality against expected results. In the world of AI, there often is no single expected result. Testers must evaluate sources, weigh input variance, and make reasoned judgments about what constitutes a “good” output. The role has evolved from enforcing rules to interpreting context. The best testers integrate multiple perspectives—business intent, user needs, ethical implications—and render informed decisions. In many ways, we’ve become both scientists and philosophers: comfortable with ambiguity, disciplined in reasoning, and courageous enough to say, “This is good enough—and this is not.”

4. Adaptability: Comfort with the Chaos

If consistency was our north star in traditional QA, adaptability is our compass in generative AI. Outputs may vary from one test run to another—and that’s not necessarily a defect. Testers must learn to distinguish between meaningful deviations and harmless variations. Structured testing approaches like “golden master” baselines, metamorphic testing, and continuous refinement cycles help us stay grounded in this flux. But beyond tools and techniques, adaptability is a mindset: accepting that uncertainty is not the enemy, but the environment. The testers who thrive are those who can pivot, learn, and keep moving forward—steady in the storm of change.

As AI systems become more powerful and less predictable, testers have the privilege—and responsibility—of shaping how humans will trust and interact with these technologies. Philosophy taught me that questioning the greats wasn’t arrogance; it was growth. The same is true for us today. In a non-deterministic world, our determination to think, question, and adapt is what turns uncertainty into excellence.

bodyHtml:
Your nonprofit has a 32% chance of technology project failure. That’s not our pessimistic guess—it’s what happens when well-meaning organizations rush into development without proper preparation. According to The Standish Group, nearly one-third of nonprofit technology initiatives fail to launch successfully, and another 40% deliver significantly less impact than originally planned.

The frustrating part is that most of these failures have nothing to do with coding skills or technical complexity. They fail because organizations skip fundamental steps that successful projects always include. We’ve guided nonprofit leaders through technology projects ranging from small-scale websites to large enterprise data platforms. The difference between success and failure isn’t budget size or technical ambition—it’s following seven specific lessons that turn good intentions into measurable impact.

Lessons Nonprofit Leaders Learned Too Late

These seven patterns emerge repeatedly in failed nonprofit technology projects. Understanding them before you start can save your organization thousands of dollars and months of frustration.

  1. Ask the Right Question First
  2. Design for Your Actual Users
  3. Right-Size Your Vision
  4. Choose Mission-Aligned Partners
  5. Nail Your Process Early
  6. Prepare Your Team for Change
  7. Invest Wisely, Not Cheaply

Let’s examine each challenge and the strategic solutions that can transform your next technology project from a costly gamble into a mission-advancing success.

Lesson 1: Ask the Right Question First

Most nonprofits approach technology projects backwards, starting with solutions rather than problems. You hear phrases like “We need a mobile app” or “We want to modernize our donor management system” before anyone has clearly defined what success actually looks like in terms of human impact.

Organizations that jump straight into technology discussions without first establishing measurable outcomes frequently build systems that work perfectly but deliver no meaningful results. According to the Project Management Institute, organizations with well-defined project goals and objectives have a 2.5 times greater chance of project success. More telling, The Standish Group found that only 29% of software projects are successful when requirements are clear, emphasizing how critical it is to define your end goal before beginning development.

Strategic Solution:

Start every technology conversation by answering this question: “What specific change in people’s lives will tell us this project succeeded?”

This means defining success in human impact terms before discussing any technical requirements.

For example, instead of “We need a client intake system,” successful organizations say: “At-risk children are now 50% more likely to meet their grade level standards” or “We are able to collect information that stops 25% of all violent crimes in a community.”

Organizations implementing this approach typically see clearer project scope, better vendor communication, and significantly higher user adoption rates. According to Wrike research, 77% of teams with clearly defined goals complete their projects on time, compared to only 46% of teams without clear goals. This impact-first thinking ensures every technical decision connects directly to mission advancement rather than technology for technology’s sake.

Lesson 2: Design for Your Actual Users

When nonprofit leaders plan technology projects, they often design solutions based on internal assumptions about what users need rather than involving actual users in the process. Organizations frequently spend months building features that look perfect in boardroom presentations but fail completely when real people try to use them.

Without early user input, technology projects regularly miss critical usability issues that could be identified and fixed affordably during the design phase. According to research by Jeff Sauro of MeasuringU, five users can identify 85% of usability problems when testing continuously. More importantly, problems found during development are ten times more expensive to fix than those caught during the design phase, as documented by Roger Pressman in “Software Engineering: A Practitioner’s Approach.”

Strategic Solution:

Bring your ideal users into the process before writing any code. Create user journey maps that visualize every step someone takes to accomplish your mission-critical goals, then validate these journeys with real people from your target audience.

For example, instead of assuming homeless individuals want a complex resource directory, successful organizations first interview people experiencing homelessness to understand their actual decision-making process when seeking help. This early feedback often reveals that simple text-based systems work better than elaborate mobile apps.

Organizations implementing this approach typically catch misalignments before expensive development begins, reduce post-launch support issues, and see significantly higher user adoption rates. According to Google research, 89% of successful businesses say anticipating customer needs and providing supportive experiences along the customer journey are critical to growth.

Lesson 3: Right-Size Your Vision

Ambitious nonprofit leaders typically want their technology to solve every problem simultaneously. We hear ambitious plans like “a comprehensive platform that manages donors, volunteers, clients, and programs while also providing mobile access and real-time reporting.” These big-picture visions sound impressive in grant proposals but consistently lead to budget overruns and failed projects.

Organizations that try to build everything simultaneously often discover that their team capacity can’t handle the complexity. As Dwight Kingdon explains in “The Magic of Small User Stories”: “Team capacity is like a funnel. When we try to force a large object (like a feature set) through it, the funnel gets clogged.” Without breaking projects into manageable pieces, teams struggle to estimate costs, timelines, and technical requirements accurately.

Strategic Solution:

Break your technology ideas into tiny pieces of functionality that can be built, tested, and delivered independently. Work from your user journey to identify the smallest possible features that still deliver meaningful value to the people you serve.

For example, instead of building a complete case management system, start with just client intake. Once that works well, add appointment scheduling. Then add progress tracking. Each piece should solve a specific problem and provide immediate value before moving to the next component.

Organizations implementing this approach typically see more accurate budget estimates, faster delivery of working features, and the ability to adjust course based on real user feedback. This incremental approach also makes it easier to identify the right technical skills needed and communicate clear requirements to development partners, reducing the risk of scope creep that destroys nonprofit technology budgets.

Lesson 4: Choose Mission-Aligned Partners

Technical skills alone don’t guarantee success in nonprofit technology projects. When nonprofit leaders search for technology partners, they often focus primarily on technical skills and budget constraints without considering whether the development team truly understands mission-driven work. Many firms excel at building e-commerce platforms or business applications but struggle to grasp the unique constraints, stakeholder dynamics, and impact measurement needs that define nonprofit technology projects.

Organizations that hire development teams without mission alignment frequently encounter partners who suggest overly complex solutions, don’t understand regulatory compliance requirements, or fail to appreciate the importance of accessibility and inclusivity in design. These mismatches lead to costly revisions, missed deadlines, and technology that serves organizational needs rather than the communities nonprofits exist to help.

Strategic Solution:

Prioritize development partners who demonstrate experience with social impact projects and can articulate how technology connects to human outcomes. Look for teams that ask about your beneficiaries, understand resource constraints, and have worked within nonprofit operational realities.

As Dr. Bettye Walker, CEO of A-MAN, Inc. STEM INTL, shared about working with QualityWorks: “The QualityWorks team took our Android educational app idea and made it a reality. They effectively managed ideation, tech team sourcing, requirements, and timelines throughout the project. They helped us innovate, simplify, and execute so we could meet our deliverables and budget.”

Organizations implementing this approach typically see better communication throughout development, fewer expensive change requests, and technology solutions that actually advance their mission. The right development partner becomes an extension of your team, helping you navigate technical decisions through the lens of social impact rather than just technical feasibility.

Lesson 5: Nail Your Process Early

Most nonprofit leaders assume their biggest technology challenges will be technical—choosing the right programming language, finding skilled developers, or managing complex integrations. However, research consistently shows that the majority of technology project failures stem from non-technical issues rather than coding problems.

According to a February 2023 Idego Group survey of software developers, 70.1% of problems in software development are non-technical, with poor management and communication being the primary culprits. Technical issues account for only 25.6% of project difficulties. Without proper project management processes, even the most skilled development teams struggle to deliver successful outcomes.

Strategic Solution:

Invest in project management systems and communication processes before investing in technology. Establish clear stakeholder roles, regular check-in schedules, decision-making protocols, and change management procedures that keep everyone aligned throughout development.

For example, successful nonprofit technology projects typically include weekly stakeholder calls, documented requirement changes, user feedback collection systems, and clear escalation paths for resolving conflicts. These processes prevent the miscommunication and scope creep that derail projects.

Organizations implementing this approach typically see projects completed on time and within budget, fewer costly revisions during development, and stronger buy-in from staff who will ultimately use the technology. As soon as you decide to create technology, you become a tech company, and every successful tech company has processes for managing technology from beginning to end. The process may be more important than the actual design and development.

Lesson 6: Prepare Your Team for Change

When nonprofit leaders plan technology implementations, they often focus exclusively on the technical aspects—software features, data migration, and system integrations—while overlooking the human side of technological change. Organizations frequently assume that if they build effective technology, people will naturally adapt and embrace it.

However, within most organizations, people’s appetite for and comfort with technology can differ immensely. Without proper change management, even the most well-designed systems fail because staff resist adoption, lack proper training, or don’t understand how the technology serves their daily work and the organization’s mission.

Strategic Solution:

Build a culture that embraces technological change before implementing new systems. Use surveys to assess your team’s technology comfort levels, create training roadmaps, and clearly communicate what’s in it for them personally and professionally.

As Sheyinka Harry, Agile Transformation Manager, explains: “Your people are the primary enablers before any new technology can add scale and speed to operations and before your customers can start realizing and experiencing the benefits of your change. With this in mind, you want to foster and encourage the exploration of new ways of thinking and working that can help to harness the power of technology to achieve your goals.”

Organizations implementing this approach typically see higher technology adoption rates, fewer support tickets and training requests, and staff who become technology advocates rather than resistors. The key is preparing your people for change before the technology arrives, not after.

Lesson 7: Invest Wisely, Not Cheaply

When nonprofit leaders evaluate technology vendors, budget constraints often drive them toward the lowest-cost option without considering the total cost of ownership. Organizations frequently focus on upfront development costs while ignoring ongoing maintenance, training, support, and potential rebuilding expenses that cheap solutions often require.

Low-cost vendors may cut corners on testing, documentation, security, or scalability—creating technical debt that becomes expensive to resolve later. Additionally, inexperienced teams often underestimate project complexity, leading to change orders, delays, and budget overruns that far exceed the initial savings.

Strategic Solution:

Evaluate technology investments based on total cost of ownership over 3-5 years, including development, training, maintenance, support, and potential future enhancements. Consider vendor experience, project management capabilities, and long-term partnership potential alongside price.

For example, a $15,000 website might seem better than a $35,000 option, but if the cheaper version requires $20,000 in fixes, security updates, and rebuilding within two years, the “expensive” option actually costs less and delivers better results.

Organizations implementing this approach typically see more predictable technology budgets, systems that scale with organizational growth, and partnerships that provide ongoing value rather than one-time transactions. Remember: in nonprofit technology, you’re not just buying code—you’re investing in your mission’s future capacity to create impact.

Moving Forward With Mission-Driven Technology

These seven lessons aren’t just theoretical frameworks—they’re hard-earned insights from watching too many well-intentioned organizations struggle with technology projects that could have succeeded with better preparation.

At QualityWorks, we’ve been privileged to partner with nonprofits ranging from local community organizations to national advocacy groups. What consistently strikes me is how much these leaders care about getting technology right, not for its own sake, but because they understand that effective technology can amplify their impact exponentially.

Every homeless individual who finds shelter through a well-designed app, every at-risk student who gets connected to mentoring through streamlined systems, every community organization that can serve twice as many families because their processes work efficiently—these outcomes justify every hour spent on proper planning and preparation.

The stakes are too high for nonprofit technology projects to fail due to preventable mistakes. Your mission deserves technology that works as hard as you do.

Simple AI wins: Steps small businesses take to compete smarter.

As a small business owner, you’re likely facing a familiar challenge: competing in markets where larger companies have specialized AI departments, dedicated tech teams, and substantial budgets — while you’re handling everything from sales calls to IT issues in the same day.

But here’s something you might not realize: your smaller size gives you a distinct advantage in AI adoption. Your business agility means you can implement AI solutions faster and with more precision than your larger, more bureaucratic competitors. According to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and Teneo, nearly all small businesses (98%) are using AI-enabled tools. This quick implementation allows you to improve your operations and customer connections immediately.

This advantage becomes even clearer when looking at larger companies’ struggles. A study by BCG found that 74% of companies have trouble achieving and scaling value from AI. Their size and complexity often slow down implementation — the exact barriers you don’t face as a smaller, more nimble business.

Why Building Your Own AI-Powered IP Matters

Are you tired of using the same off-the-shelf software as everyone else in your industry? When all your competitors use identical tools, what really sets you apart?

When you purchase off-the-shelf AI solutions, you’re getting the same capabilities as everyone else. There’s no competitive edge to be found there. But developing custom AI solutions tailored to your specific business challenges creates intellectual property that belongs exclusively to your company.

Unlike subscription software where you’re essentially renting access, custom-developed AI becomes your intellectual property—a business asset that grows in value over time and creates something competitors can’t easily replicate.

Real-World AI Applications You Can Implement

  1. Customer Insights and Retention

Imagine being able to predict which customers are likely to leave before they show any obvious signs. Companies face this challenge daily when relying on traditional monitoring methods.

AI solutions can analyze your specific customer data patterns to identify at-risk clients before traditional metrics would catch them.

A financial services company similar implemented this approach with impressive results. They achieved a 7x faster time-to-market for new digital services and captured 30x more customer feedback before launch. Their customer satisfaction scores increased while development costs decreased—all without hiring a single additional staff member.

  1. Know Your Process Gaps

Picture reducing your most time-consuming testing and quality assurance processes from days to minutes. Mid-sized companies often struggle with overwhelming quality assurance demands that slow down their entire development cycle. AI-powered automation frameworks can transform these bottlenecks. Studies by Boston Consulting Group (BCG) show that automation has improved jobs for 90% of knowledge workers and increased productivity for 66% of them.

For example, one mid-sized software company implemented AI testing automation with impressive results. Their testing time dropped from 4 days to just 45 minutes, team workload decreased by 30%, and their release cycle shortened by 25%. These efficiencies freed their team to focus on growth initiatives rather than maintenance tasks.

Making AI Accessible for Your Business

You might think you need a full technical team to leverage AI. That’s simply not true. Fractional technical leadership allows you to access strategic guidance without the full-time executive cost.

With the right technical advisor, you can:

  • Identify where AI would deliver the most immediate value for your specific business
  • Design a roadmap that builds your AI capabilities in manageable phases
  • Find the right development resources that fit your budget
  • Ensure your AI solutions create lasting proprietary value

Even a few hours of expert guidance monthly can help you avoid costly mistakes and ensure your AI investments build lasting business value.

5 Steps to Start Building Your AI Advantage

Ready to move forward? Here’s how to begin:

  1. Identify Your Highest-Value Problem
    Look for processes where you’re manually handling data, making routine decisions, or responding to predictable situations. These are prime candidates for AI enhancement.
  2. Take Inventory of Your Data Assets
    What customer, operational, or market data do you already collect? Good AI needs good data, so understanding what you have is critical.
  3. Set Clear Success Metrics
    Define exactly how you’ll measure the impact. Is it reducing a specific cost? Increasing customer retention? Accelerating a process? Specific targets make success measurable.
  4. Start Small and Targeted
    Your first AI project should deliver visible results within 3-4 months. Focus on a narrow use case you can implement quickly, then expand from that foundation.
  5. Build for Ownership
    Ensure your contracts with developers give you complete ownership of the solution. The intellectual property value often exceeds the immediate operational benefits.

Addressing Your ROI Concerns

Let’s talk about what’s likely on your mind—cost. Custom software development isn’t cheap, but neither is falling behind competitors who are leveraging AI.

Consider starting with a hybrid approach. Many small businesses begin with a modified off-the-shelf solution that’s customized to their specific needs. This delivers immediate benefits while building toward more proprietary solutions.

According to industry research from TrueList’s “Software Testing Statistics 2024”, approximately 35% of companies now involve existing team members in software testing tasks rather than hiring specialists. This approach allows you to leverage AI for testing and quality assurance without expanding your headcount.

Your Next Move

As a small business owner, starting to build AI-powered IP now will create advantages that get harder for competitors to overcome with each passing year. The technical barriers to entry have never been lower, but the window of opportunity won’t stay open forever.

Think about your specific business challenges. Where are you spending too much time on repetitive tasks? Which processes could benefit from prediction or automation? Where could better data insights give you an edge?

bodyHtml:
Testing needed: Discover tactical ways to use AI and best practice services to support testing without sacrificing development time and budget.

The Reality of Quality Assurance in Today’s Engineering Teams

According to TrueList’s “Software Testing Statistics 2024”, approximately 35% of companies involve non-testers such as developers or other staff members in software testing tasks. Many engineering teams operate with limited or no dedicated QA resources at all.

While developers should certainly take ownership of their code quality, it’s unrealistic and unfair to expect them to possess the specialized testing knowledge of QA professionals without proper support systems. The good news? With today’s AI-powered tools and strategic approaches, organizations can achieve exceptional quality outcomes even without a dedicated testing department. 

At QualityWorks Consulting Group, we’ve worked with organizations across the spectrum of quality assurance approaches. While we advocate for the value of specialized testing expertise, we also recognize the practical constraints many engineering leaders face today: tight budgets, competing priorities, and organizational decisions that place quality responsibility entirely on development teams.

This article provides practical strategies using AI and targeted services to help development organizations achieve quality outcomes with their current resources.

Challenges Engineering Leaders Face Without Dedicated QA

We’ll cover four critical challenges with solutions you can implement before year-end:

  1. Too Many Bugs in Production
    Too Many Bugs Reaching Customers Due to Limited Test Coverage
  2. Delayed Product Releases
    Developers Struggling to Balance Coding and Testing, Delaying Releases
  3. No Quality Metrics
    No Consistent Quality Processes or Metrics to Guide Improvement
  4. Requirements Don’t Match Reality
    Features Don’t Match Requirements, Leading to Customer Dissatisfaction

Let’s dig into each problem and the targeted solutions that can turn things around quickly. Aww

Challenge #1: Too Many Bugs in Production

When development teams lack QA specialists, testing often becomes a secondary priority when delivery pressure mounts. Studies show that organizations relying solely on developer testing frequently experience lower test coverage and more defects making it to production.

Recommended Solution: Use AI to generate comprehensive test cases that target critical functionality. Tools like Testers.ai can quickly analyze your application and generate test scenarios that developers might not consider, including edge cases. These AI-generated test cases provide a ready-made testing framework that developers can execute without spending hours creating test plans.

For example, we’ve worked with engineering teams who feed their requirements into AI testing tools and receive complete test suites covering positive, negative, and boundary scenarios – significantly expanding coverage with minimal time investment.

Challenge #2: Delayed Product Releases 

When developers handle both feature development and thorough testing, development velocity often slows significantly. This dual responsibility creates bottlenecks that lead to missed deadlines and delayed releases.

Recommended Solution: Implement AI-powered test automation that generates and maintains test scripts. QualityWatcher AI’s Test Case to Automation tool can transform test cases into working code that integrates with project management systems.

An effective approach involves:

  1. Using AI to generate test cases from requirements
  2. Converting those test cases into automation scripts
  3. Integrating these tests into your CI/CD pipeline

Organizations implementing this approach typically see reduced testing time while maintaining effective defect detection. This allows developers to focus more on building features rather than extensive manual testing.

Challenge #3: No Quality Metrics

Without a QA team establishing standards, many organizations operate in a quality vacuum – no formalized testing processes, no structured defect tracking, and no meaningful metrics to show if things are actually improving. This lack of framework makes it virtually impossible to systematically raise quality, measure progress, or quantify the business impact of quality issues.

Recommended Solution: Bring in test architecture experts to build your quality foundation. These specialized consultants can:

  • Design testing infrastructure tailored to your specific technology stack
  • Implement appropriate test management systems
  • Develop AI test models customized for your products
  • Train your developers in efficient testing approaches that won’t slow them down

Our work with dozens of engineering teams reveals a common pattern: organizations expect developers to own code quality but rarely equip them with the testing knowledge needed for success. Most developers weren’t trained in comprehensive testing methodologies – it’s not their primary expertise and shouldn’t be.

Test architecture services evaluate your specific needs, identify the right tooling, implement automation frameworks, and train your team – all without requiring permanent QA staffing.

Challenge #4: Requirements Don’t Match Reality

Without dedicated verification of requirements throughout development, products often drift from specifications and user expectations. This misalignment between promised functionality and actual delivery creates customer frustration, support tickets, and expensive post-release fixes.

Recommended Solution: Formalize user acceptance testing with AI-generated test plans. By providing requirements and specifications to language models with specific prompts, teams can create structured test plans aligned with intended functionality.

A simple prompt like: “Based on these requirements, create a detailed acceptance test plan” can generate comprehensive testing guidance that helps keep development aligned with requirements.

Making user testing more structured helps identify issues earlier:

  • Use QualityWatcher AI to create clear testing instructions
  • Generate targeted scenarios focusing on critical functions
  • Implement structured feedback mechanisms

Organizations using this approach typically find misalignments before products reach customers, reducing post-release support issues.

Implementation Steps for Engineering Leaders

If you’re leading a development team without QA resources, here’s a practical implementation roadmap:

  1. Use AI to Generate Test Cases – Leverage AI tools to create comprehensive test plans based on requirements and specifications.
  2. Use AI to Automate Tests and Integrate into CI/CD pipeline – Make testing an automatic part of your deployment pipeline rather than a separate activity that can be skipped.
  3. Invest in Test Architecture – A small upfront investment in proper testing architecture will pay dividends through reduced bugs and faster releases.
  4. Use AI to Make User Testing More Structured – Generate plans that give users clarity on what and how they can help, ensuring critical bugs are found during testing, not in production.

Moving Forward With Developer-Led Quality

While specialized QA teams certainly add value, developer-led testing becomes remarkably effective when powered by the right AI tools, automation support, and occasional expert guidance. The secret isn’t eliminating testing – it’s making testing smarter, faster, and less disruptive to development work.

Forward-thinking engineering leaders can maintain exceptional quality standards without dedicated QA staff by strategically deploying AI for test generation and automation, establishing proper testing infrastructure, and bringing in targeted expertise to solve specific quality challenges.
